facts.headline: The bookcase that hid a family for two years still swings open
facts.body_html: In 1942, a helper built a revolving bookcase to conceal the entrance to the Secret Annex — the only way in or out for the eight people hiding behind it. It's still there, and you can still walk through it.

facts.headline: Rembrandt's masterpiece was trimmed to fit through a door
facts.body_html: In 1715, movers cut strips off all four sides of The Night Watch — including two figures on the left — just to squeeze it between two doors at the old Town Hall. The missing pieces were digitally restored 300 years later.

facts.headline: Amsterdam's palace stands on 13,659 wooden piles
facts.body_html: Built on marshland in the 1600s, the Royal Palace on Dam Square is held up by 13,659 wooden piles driven deep into the soil — locals called it the "Eighth Wonder of the World" when it opened as a town hall.

facts.headline: Rembrandt's grave has never been found
facts.body_html: He was buried inside Westerkerk in 1669, but as a pauper his remains were cleared after 20 years — nobody knows exactly where he lies. The tower above still wears a blue replica crown gifted by an emperor in 1489.

facts.headline: A 500-year-old wooden house hides behind these walls
facts.body_html: Step through the gate into the Begijnhof and find Het Houten Huys, built around 1528 — one of only two wooden-fronted houses left after the city banned wood facades to stop fires.

facts.headline: This house is barely wider than its own front door
facts.body_html: Singel 7's canal-facing wall is just over a meter wide — built that narrow because Amsterdammers were taxed on canal frontage. The house actually widens to 5 meters once you're inside.

facts.headline: Up to 15,000 bikes get pulled out of the canals every year
facts.body_html: Amsterdam holds the Guinness World Record for bicycles fished from a city's waterways — claw-armed barges haul thousands out annually, mostly stolen or dumped.
